# Opening Case: Christ Had No Biological Father

**Definition.** By "biological father" I mean a man whose seed (Greek *sperma*, "seed"; Hebrew *zera'*, "seed") begot the child. The question is whether the KJV text gives Christ such a father. I hold that it does not. Joseph was the husband of Mary and the reputed, legal father. The conception was of the Holy Ghost in Mary alone.

---

## I. Matthew 1 breaks its own pattern at verse 16

**[L1]** Matthew 1:2-16 reads "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob…" down to verse 16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** The verb in every "begat" is *egennēsen* (Greek, "he begat," the active verb of a father's act). In verse 16 the verb changes to *egennēthē* (Greek, "was born," passive). The relative phrase is *ex hēs* (Greek, "out of whom"), in the feminine singular. It points to Mary alone and cannot include Joseph. Joseph is called *ton andra Marias* (Greek, "the husband of Mary"), not the one who begat.

**[L4]** The chain: the repeated active "begat" in 1:2-16 [L1], plus the switch to the passive with a feminine singular antecedent in 1:16 [L2], gives the inference that Matthew deliberately withholds "begat" from Joseph's relation to Jesus. Each earlier name "begat" the next, and this one does not.

## II. The conception was "of the Holy Ghost"

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "…before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost." Verse 20: "…that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Ek pneumatos hagiou* (Greek, "out of Holy Spirit") uses *ek* (Greek, "out of"), the preposition of source. *Gennēthen* (Greek, "that which is begotten or conceived") in 1:20 is the same root as the "begat" of the genealogy, and here its source is the Spirit. *Episkiasei* (Greek, "will overshadow") is the verb of divine presence and power. In Exodus 40:35 the cloud "abode thereon" and the glory filled the tabernacle, and the Septuagint uses the same root there (*episkiazō*).

**[L3]** Luke 1:35 says *dio kai* (Greek, "therefore also"), which makes the manner of conception the stated ground of the child's title. Matthew 1:20 and Luke 1:35 agree independently on the source.

## III. Mary was a virgin before and through the conception

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son." Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child."

**[L2]** *Ou ginōskō* (Greek, "I know not," meaning no sexual knowledge) is Mary's own statement. *Parthenos* (Greek, "virgin") is the word Matthew uses to render Isaiah 7:14. The Hebrew *ha-'almāh* (Hebrew, "the young woman") is a lexeme of age and marriageability, not of explicit virginity. Isaiah 7:11, 14 resolves the sense: the Lord gives *'ōth* (Hebrew, "a sign") that could be asked "in the depth, or in the height above." An ordinary conception is no sign. The Spirit-inspired citation in Matthew 1:22-23 fixes the sense as *parthenos*.

**[L3]** Genesis 24:16 describes Rebekah as *bethulah* (Hebrew, "virgin"), "neither had any man known her," which shows how Scripture states virginity when it wants to. Matthew 1:25 uses the same idiom, "knew her not," with *heōs hou* (Greek, "until"). It limits the statement to before the birth, so that the conception cannot be credited to Joseph.

## IV. Joseph is the reputed father, not the begetter

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "Jesus… being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph." Luke 2:48-49: "Thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." Jesus answers: "Wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" Matthew 1:20-21, 25: Joseph is told to take Mary as wife, and he "called his name JESUS."

**[L2]** *Enomizeto* (Greek, "was supposed, was reckoned by custom or law") marks an opinion, not a fact of begetting. Luke's parenthesis exists to correct the popular view. Joseph's naming of the child is an act of legal acknowledgment.

**[L3]** John 6:42 ("Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph?") records the crowd's assumption. The text does not endorse it. Matthew 1:19 shows Joseph "minded to put her away privily," which is the reaction of a man who knows he is not the father.

**[L4]** Luke 2:48-49 gives the title "father" to Joseph in Mary's mouth [L1], and the child immediately transfers the word to God [L1]. Luke 3:23's *enomizeto* marks Joseph's as a reputed relation [L2]. From these the inference follows that "father" for Joseph is a legal and household usage, not a biological claim.

## V. The wider witness

**[L1]** Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman." Hebrews 10:5: "a body hast thou prepared me." Acts 2:30: "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne." Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh."

**[L2]** *Genomenon ek gunaikos* (Greek, "come to be out of a woman") names only the mother as source. *Katērtisō* (Greek, "thou hast fitted or prepared") makes the body something God prepared. In Romans 1:3 and Acts 2:30, *sperma* (Greek, "seed") and *osphus* (Greek, "loins") trace descent to David, and the descent is traced through Mary, not Joseph.

**[L3]** Genesis 3:15 speaks of "her seed," the woman's, which is the only place in Genesis where seed is assigned to a woman without a man. Jeremiah 31:22 says "a woman shall compass a man," a new thing in the earth. These agree with the NT witness.

**[L4]** Romans 1:3 and Acts 2:30 anticipate the objection that Davidic "seed" requires Joseph. Matthew 1:12 places Joseph in the line of Jechonias, and Jeremiah 22:30 says none of Coniah's "seed" shall prosper, "sitting upon the throne of David." Joseph's line therefore carries the legal claim, and Luke 1:27-35 locates the actual conception in Mary. Together these footings support the inference that the throne-right passed legally through Joseph while the bodily descent passed through Mary.

---

## DECLARED CHAIN -- the links your case stands on

1. Matthew 1:16 breaks the "begat" pattern of 1:2-15 and names Mary alone as the one "of whom was born" Jesus. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:2-16; [L2] *egennēsen* (he begat) against *egennēthē ex hēs* (was born out of whom, feminine singular).
2. The conception is sourced in the Holy Ghost, not in a man. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:18, 20; Luke 1:35; [L2] *ek pneumatos hagiou* (out of Holy Spirit), *episkiasei* (will overshadow); [L3] the two accounts agree independently.
3. Mary was a virgin through the conception, and Isaiah 7:14 foretold it as a sign. Footing: [L1] Luke 1:34; Matthew 1:23, 25; [L2] *ou ginōskō* (I know not a man), *parthenos* (virgin), *'ōth* (sign); [L3] Isaiah 7:11, 14; Genesis 24:16.
4. Joseph is the reputed and legal father only. Footing: [L1] Luke 3:23; Luke 2:48-49; Matthew 1:19-21, 25; [L2] *enomizeto* (was supposed); [L3] John 6:42 as the crowd's assumption.
5. The wider Scripture assigns Christ's flesh to the woman and to God's preparing, not to a human father. Footing: [L1] Galatians 4:4; Hebrews 10:5; Acts 2:30; [L2] *genomenon ek gunaikos* (come to be out of a woman), *katērtisō* (thou hast prepared); [L3] Genesis 3:15; Jeremiah 31:22.
6. Christ had no biological father: Joseph did not beget him, and the conception was of the Holy Ghost in Mary alone. Footing: links 1-5, with [L1] Matthew 1:16, 18-20, 25; Luke 1:34-35; [L2] *egennēthē ex hēs* (was born out of whom), *ek pneumatos hagiou* (out of Holy Spirit).

**[L3]** Genesis 4:1 gives the canon's means of begetting, "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived." Matthew 1:25 uses the same idiom negated, *ouk eginōsken* (Greek, "he was not knowing"). **[L1]** The challenger cites John 1:13, "born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God." **[L2]** The word there is *andros* (Greek, "of a male"). **[L1]** The challenger offers Solomon (2 Samuel 7:14; 1 Chronicles 28:6) as a case where God is called father of a man David begat. **[L3]** In Solomon's case the text states David's begetting elsewhere (2 Samuel 12:24, "he went in unto her, and lay with her: and she bare a son"). **[L1]** Matthew 1:22-23 says "Now **all this** was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying, Behold, a virgin shall be with child." The same woman is *'almah* in verse 43 and *bethulah* (Hebrew, "virgin") in verse 16. **[L4]** The word is therefore used of a verified virgin (Genesis 24:43 with 24:16) [L1, L3] and does not exclude virginity in Isaiah 7:14. ---

**[L2]** The verb *nomizō* (Greek, "to suppose, reckon") appears in the very rows the challenger cites and elsewhere, and its rows are mistaken suppositions: Luke 2:44, "supposing him to have been in the company" (he was in Jerusalem); Acts 14:19, "supposing he had been dead" (he was not); Acts 16:27, "supposing that the prisoners had been fled" (they were not); Acts 21:29, "whom they supposed that Paul had brought into the temple" (he had not). **[L4]** The challenger's own Luke 2:44, with Acts 14:19, 16:27 and 21:29 [L1], shows the supposition in that verb's rows was false or merely held as opinion. So counting by the father's house does not prove begetting.

**[L1]** On "parents" (Luke 2:27, 41): in the same chapter Luke 2:33 reads "Joseph and his mother." The child's answer to "thy father" is "my Father's business" (Luke 2:48-49). **[L4]** Mary's "thy father" and the child's "my Father" stand side by side (Luke 2:48-49) [L1], and Luke 3:23's parenthesis marks the first as reputation [L2]. **[L1]** Luke 3:23 gives the head of the line as "Joseph, which was of Heli." Matthew 1:16 says "Jacob begat Joseph." **[L2]** In Luke 3:23-38 the Greek gives the word *huios* (Greek, "son") only once, at the head, with the qualifier "as was supposed." The challenger says Ezra 2:61-62 refuses the wife's house. **[L1]** The verses say the priests "sought their register among those that were reckoned by genealogy, but they were not found." The exclusion followed the missing register, not the wife's house. Verse 61 itself says the man "was called after their name."

**[L3]** On Luke 1:36, Elisabeth "of the daughters of Aaron" does not bar Mary from Judah, since Exodus 6:23 has Aaron take Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab, and Numbers 2:3 sets Amminadab's house in Judah. **[L1]** On the idiom "made of a woman" (Galatians 4:4), I re-seat it in its chain. Galatians 4:4 names the one source, "of a woman." Genesis 3:15 and Jeremiah 31:22 are supporting rows. Link 5 does not rest on them alone.
